title: Non-vanishing of Geodesic Periods of Automorphic Forms
summary: The real Gaussian mass estimate in (5.2) has the wrong exponent; the exact-zero5/4 deduction can be repaired. The graph transform loses isolated-vertex mass, with explicit modular examples at arbitrarily large N. A continuous unbounded density disproves the general uniform transfer rate. The Eisenstein scaling remains a named unresolved input.

problems.title: The one-dimensional Gaussian mass in (5.2) is incorrectly bounded by the square of the interval radius
problems.source_location: Theorem 3.4, p.17; Theorem 5.1 and (5.2), p.25; optimization p.26.
problems.claim: Theorem5.1's stated exponent is obtained by (5.2)'s squared-radius Gaussian estimate.
hypotheses: Real one-dimensional Maaß-period Gaussian input of Theorem3.4, uniform interval error O((log N)^(-1/2)).
delta>0; alpha=1+min(delta,1/4); comparison error O(1) along edges.
complete_check: For the standard real Gaussian density φ(x)=(2π)^(-1/2)e^(−x^2/2), integral_(-r)^r φ(x)dx=sqrt(2/π)r+O(r^3) as r→0.

In (5.2), r=c''(log N)^(−(α−1)) with α−1>0, whereas the printed final upper bound is O((log N)^(−2(α−1))). The ratio of the Gaussian mass to that proposed bound grows like a positive constant times (log N)^(α−1).
For example, δ=1/8 gives α−1=1/8, so the mass has order (log N)^(−1/8), not O((log N)^(−1/4)). The Berry–Esseen error O((log N)^(−1/2)) cannot correct this mismatch.
A two-dimensional Gaussian small-ball estimate would have quadratic radius behavior, but the cited input and the theorem under proof are explicitly one-dimensional real Hecke-Maaß periods.
problems.calculation_type: Exact analytic Gaussian expansion and degree optimization.
problems.counterevidence: The direct exact-zero argument recovers Theorem 1.3's 5/4 exponent. The qualitative cusp-form result uses only o(1) small/large-period probabilities and is not undermined by this squared-radius mistake. No actual Maaß form or geodesic family contradicting the stronger theorem has been produced.
problems.repair: Correct (5.2) and revise the quantitative small-period bound to the checked exponent, or supply a new argument establishing the stronger exponent. For δ≥1/2 retain the O(1) comparison term rather than absorbing it into a decaying threshold.
problems.repair_verification: The weaker exponent1+min(delta/2,1/4) and the exact-zero5/4 argument are explicitly checked conditional on period comparison, counting and sparse equidistribution inputs; theorem truth in the stronger range is not disproved.
problems.impact: The displayed proof does not establish Theorem 5.1's exponent 1+min(δ,1/4) for 0<δ<1/2. The checked available argument instead gives 1+min(δ/2,1/4). Additional information or a different argument is needed for the stronger stated range.
problems.severity_reason: An invalid central estimate leaves the stated quantitative strengthening unsupported; this is a proof gap rather than a claimed counterexample to the theorem.

problems.title: The actual graph transform is not automatically a probability measure
problems.source_location: Definitions§4.1 p18; graph(4.1)–(4.5) pp18–19; (6.1),Lemma6.1 pp28–29; application§6.3 pp31–32
problems.claim: For any probability measure mu on X, the specified G(mu) has total mass1 and mu(e^-1(B))≤G(mu)(B).
hypotheses: I={x:deg(x)=0}; e^-1(B) includes all vertices whose entire neighbour set is contained in B, including empty sets.
The actual graph has X_N double cosets with0<c≤N and Y_N classes with N/2≤absolute trace≤N; mu_N is uniform on X_N.
complete_check: Summing(6.1) gives G(mu)(Y)=sum_(deg x>0)mu(x)=1−mu(I). WithB=Y, e^-1(Y)=X, so Lemma6.1's lower bound fails ifmu(I)>0.

AtN=21, gamma=[[-6,-5],[17,14]] has determinant1,c17 andtrace8. Left/right integral unipotents give all traces8+17k. The two closest are8,−9 and the next have absolute value≥25, so no trace lies in[10.5,21]; this vertex is isolated.

For everyinteger m≥12, gamma_m=[[m+1,1],[2m+1,2]], N_m=floor(5(2m+1)/4). Determinant1, c≤N. Trace progressionm+3+k(2m+1) has closest valuesm+3,2−m both belowN/2 in absolute value, and all others aboveN. Thus isolation occurs at arbitrarily largeN.
problems.calculation_type: Direct matrix determinant, double-coset trace formula and summation; no executed numerical experiment.
problems.counterevidence: A positive mass for each finiteN does not imply positive limiting mass. No asymptotic counterexample to Theorem1.9 is asserted. The unweighted §5 edge-count proof does not require normalization and ignores isolated vertices.
problems.repair: Require mu(I)=0 for the abstract lemma. For the actual graph, condition on nonisolated vertices or change the construction, and establish the necessary isolated-mass estimate. The distributional comparison then includes O(zeta_N) for zeta_N=mu_N(I_N).
problems.repair_verification: The total-mass identity and conditional-normalization error are checked. zeta_N=o(1), its effective rate and a modified graph theorem remain unverified.
problems.impact: Exact probability and lower-preimage claims are false as written; the transfer route for a main weighted-distribution statement needs missing normalization control.
problems.severity_reason: The missing condition is used in the main weighted-distribution deduction and demonstrably fails in its actual graphs. Grade refers to that proof/definition gap, not a claim that the limiting theorem is false.

problems.title: Continuity of a density does not imply the uniform O(E) endpoint estimate
problems.claim: For every continuous probability densityF the interval comparison is uniformly O_F(h(n)+E(n)).
hypotheses: Disjoint triangular spikes give a locally finite continuous density with total integral sum2^(−j)=1 and unbounded heights.
For eachn choose a finite midpoint-quantile approximation with uniform interval errorh(n)≤w_n². Take a matching graph between two copies, f_n equal to quantiles andg_n=f_n+w_n.
complete_check: Every vertex has degree1, so the graph transform is a probability measure and every edge error isE(n)=w_n.
On[0,3n], the shifted empirical mass differs from the target by integral_(3n−w_n)^(3n)F+O(h(n))=n w_n/2+O(w_n²).
Dividing byh(n)+E(n) yields a quantity tending to infinity. This is an exact counterexample to the uniformly quantified lemma with every stated assumption satisfied.
problems.calculation_type: Analytic fixed-density/finite-quantile construction; no numerical test.
problems.counterevidence: The standard Gaussian is bounded, so a bounded-density correction works for the intended Gaussian input. It does not repair the separate isolated-mass issue.
problems.repair: Assume F is bounded, or replaceO(E) by the uniform concentration modulus sup_b integral_b^(b+O(E))F. The latter tends to0 for integrableF, but need not beO(E).
problems.repair_verification: A boundedF gives interval mass≤||F||∞times interval length. The counterexample proves continuity alone is insufficient.
problems.impact: False general auxiliary rate; Gaussian specialization survives this density correction subject to the separate graph hypotheses.
problems.severity_reason: A stronger hypothesis already holds for the specific Gaussian density, so this general-lemma defect is local.

needs_evidence.subject: Eisenstein normalization
needs_evidence.details: Theorem3.5 prints c_E*sqrt(log N), while§5 andTheorem1.6 use an extra(log log N)^(3/2) or(log X)^(3/2). The external cited theorem was not inspected; do not choose or certify one scale without evidence.

checked_non_problem_annotations.name: The degree upper bound actually needed by the edge argument
reasoning: Every representative of a double coset differs by left and right integral unipotents, so its trace lies in a+d+kc(x). The number of such progression values in the two intervals [N/2,N] and [−N,−N/2] is at most N/c(x)+2. The number of distinct conjugacy classes is at most that number. Thus deg(x)≤N/c(x)+2, without requiring that all these classes be distinct.
Let M(t)=#{x:c(x)≤t}. From the supplied M(t)=O(t^2), partial summation gives sum_(c(x)≤t) 1/c(x)=O(t); for 1≤t≤N, therefore sum_(c(x)≤t)deg(x)=O(Nt).
For any B⊂X_N and any cutoff 1≤t≤N, sum_(x∈B)deg(x)≤O(Nt)+O((N/t+1)|B|). This is the estimate needed in §5.
checked_non_problem_annotations.result: The required one-sided estimate and the cutoff calculation are checked conditional on the stated double-coset counting asymptotic.
checked_non_problem_annotations.limits: This contribution does not certify the exact equality (4.6), the two-sided error claimed in Lemma 4.1, or non-isolation of X_N. In particular, isolated vertices contribute zero to these degree sums and do not obstruct this one-sided argument.

checked_non_problem_annotations.name: Geometric lower-degree mechanism
reasoning: For a radius-r semicircle, its hyperbolic length above height M is 2 arcosh(r/M) when r≥M. The length between heights M and 2M is bounded by 2 log(2+sqrt(3)): it increases to that value for r≤2M and decreases for r≥2M.
An axis meeting the fixed strip B has radius at least M_Γ≥1. Since r=sqrt(tr(γ)^2−4)/(2|c_γ|), this forces |c_γ|≤|tr(γ)|≤N, so the corresponding double coset is an actual neighbour.

Matrices in a fixed double coset and fixed PSL conjugacy class have at most two possible lifted traces. For each fixed lifted trace, the trace progression forces a fixed sum of left/right translation parameters, leaving a single Γ_∞-conjugation family. Hence there are at most a fixed number of translation families per edge. Each contributes O(1) strip length by the semicircle bound.
This yields length(C_y∩B)=O(deg(y)), as needed, allowing harmless absolute factors for the two possible lift signs.
checked_non_problem_annotations.result: The geometric constant-bound mechanism needed for Proposition 4.2 is checked.
checked_non_problem_annotations.limits: This is not a claim that every literal representative/sign sentence in the printed proof is exact. The argument only requires an absolute constant. Primitive axes and the stated cusp embedding remain part of the source setup.

checked_non_problem_annotations.name: Sparse equidistribution and its application threshold
reasoning: For a zero-mean bounded continuous φ, flow invariance replaces its integral on each closed orbit by the integral of φ_T. The length-proportion assumption gives an upper bound ε^(-1) times the full collection average of |φ_T|. First take X→∞ at fixed T using full-collection equidistribution; then T→∞ using the L1 ergodic theorem. This proves the stated positive-length-proportion implication conditionally on those two inputs.

In the modular sparse argument, the discarded discriminants have length at most O(e^(5X/6)+sqrt(ψ(X))length(C(X))/X). Dividing by length(I_X)≥ψ(X)length(C(X))/X makes these terms O(X e^(−X/6)/ψ(X))+O(ψ(X)^(-1/2)), both tending to zero.

The remaining discriminant subcollections satisfy the stated relative-length threshold for the cited Aka–Einsiedler theorem because ψ can be replaced by an increasing minorant, X≥log(D/4), and log length(C_D)≤log D for large D. The averaging step is valid once that external uniform sparse-equidistribution input is available.

At X≈2 log N, a hypothetical exceptional set of size at least a constant times N^2/(log N)^(1+κ), with κ≤1/4, has total length at least a constant times N^2/(log N)^κ. Relative to the threshold length(C(X))/X≈N^2/log N, the extra factor is of order (log N)^(1−κ)→∞. Thus the sparse theorem applies to the sets used in the corrected quantitative argument.
checked_non_problem_annotations.result: The internal two-limit and mass-discarding deductions are checked; the external equidistribution theorems themselves are not independently proved.
checked_non_problem_annotations.limits: The Aka–Einsiedler theorem, full prime-geodesic equidistribution, geodesic-flow ergodicity and class-number/counting results are declared dependencies.

checked_non_problem_annotations.name: Corrected quantitative edge count and exact-zero counterevidence
reasoning: Write L=log N and ρ=min(δ,1/2). Proposition 3.1 gives |L_f(x)|≤L^(1/2−δ)+O(1)=O(L^(1/2−ρ)) for neighbours of periods in the stated small-period set. The O(1) term must be retained when δ>1/2.
The real Gaussian CLT in Theorem 3.4 then gives |B_N|/|X_N|=O(L^(−ρ)+L^(−1/2))=O(L^(−ρ)), since real Gaussian small-interval mass is proportional to its radius.

Choose t=N/L^(ρ/2) in the checked one-sided degree bound. Both Nt and (N/t)|B_N| are O(N^2/L^(ρ/2)). The sparse geometric lower bound is sum_(y∈A_N)deg(y)≫|A_N|L when A_N is at least the target order; otherwise the target bound already holds.
It follows from these inputs that |A_N|=O(N^2/L^(1+ρ/2))=O(N^2/L^(1+min(δ/2,1/4))). This is weaker than the printed Theorem 5.1 for 0<δ<1/2.
For exact zeros, Proposition 3.1 gives |L_f(x)|=O(1) directly. Then |B_N|=O(N^2/L^(1/2)), the cutoff is t=N/L^(1/4), and the same argument gives |A_N^0|=O(N^2/L^(5/4)).

The passage to geodesic length uses |tr(γ)|=2 cosh(length(C_γ)/2), so N is comparable to e^(X/2). Summing the dyadic trace bounds gives O(e^X/X^(5/4)); the small-trace tail is of smaller order. Thus the exact-zero headline bound can be recovered without the invalid squared-radius step.
checked_non_problem_annotations.result: A genuine quantitative proof gap is isolated, and the checked zero-period argument preserves the stated headline exponent conditional on the named source inputs.
checked_non_problem_annotations.limits: No counterexample to the truth of Theorem 5.1 is claimed. The weaker small-period estimate and the exact-zero repair are new analytic deductions in this bounded contribution, not independent acceptance of the paper.

checked_non_problem_annotations.name: Qualitative density-one deduction for the cuspidal cases
reasoning: For cusp forms, the uniform O(1) comparison along an edge is negligible relative to sqrt(log N)/h(N) after replacing h by a slower positive minorant if necessary.

Weak convergence to the real or complex Gaussian, absence of an atom at zero, and tightness imply that the fraction of X_N with normalized periods below 1/h(N) or above h(N) tends to zero. This follows by comparison with fixed small/large rectangles or intervals, so it does not require an unsupported moving-window consequence of pointwise convergence.
If m_N=|B_N|/N^2→0, choose ψ(N)→∞ slowly enough that m_N ψ(N)→0. The degree upper bound with t=N/ψ(N) gives total incident edge mass o(N^2).

If the exceptional geodesics have positive proportion, their total length has positive proportion, so Theorem 4.5 and Proposition 4.2 give an edge lower bound of order N^2, a contradiction. If the source's set D_N={c(x)≤N/sqrt(log N)} is removed, its total degree is O(N^2/sqrt(log N))=o(N^2), so the contradiction remains.
Isolated X_N vertices have degree zero and are irrelevant to this edge-sum contradiction; no probability normalization of a graph transform is needed.
checked_non_problem_annotations.result: The qualitative cusp-form argument is coherent conditional on the source's period comparison, CLTs and equidistribution inputs.
checked_non_problem_annotations.limits: The Eisenstein case is excluded from this positive conclusion because its displayed normalizing factors are inconsistent in the source and require separate resolution.

checks.source_claim: Theorem 5.1 and equation (5.2), physical PDF 25, with the explicitly real one-dimensional uniform Gaussian input in Theorem 3.4 on page 17 and degree optimization on page 26.
checks.independent_reasoning: For r>0 tending to zero, integrating the real standard normal density gives sqrt(2/pi) r+O(r^3). At delta=1/8 the source chooses alpha-1=1/8 and r=c''(log N)^-1/8, so the integral is of order (log N)^-1/8; it is not O((log N)^-1/4). The uniform O((log N)^-1/2) CLT error is smaller and cannot make this upper-bound step valid. The source's actual theorem is about real MaaÃŸ periods, so a complex two-dimensional small-ball estimate is inapplicable.
checks.counterevidence_and_repair: I independently checked the report's corrected argument against Proposition 3.1 (page 14), the graph/counting definitions (18-20), and the sparse threshold (23-24). Write rho=min(delta,1/2). Because c<=N and |trace|>=N/2, the period-comparison error is O(1), giving |B_N|=O(N^2(log N)^-rho). In a fixed double coset, representatives with the same signed trace are unipotently conjugate, hence deg(x)<=N/c(x)+2 is valid even if some signed traces give the same PSL conjugacy class. With M(t)=O(t^2), partial summation gives sum_(c<=t)1/c=O(t), so incident edges are O(Nt+(N/t+1)|B_N|). Choosing t=N/(log N)^(rho/2) yields O(N^2/(log N)^(rho/2)). When |A_N| is at least its target scale, total length exceeds the sparse threshold by a diverging power (log N)^(1-rho/2), and Proposition 4.2 plus Theorem 4.6 gives at least a constant times |A_N| log N edges. The resulting exponent is 1+min(delta/2,1/4). For exact zeros the O(1) comparison gives rho=1/2 directly, recovering 5/4; the exact trace-length relation and dyadic sum give the headline O(exp(X)/X^(5/4)). These are conditional deductions from the named source inputs, not fresh proofs of external CLTs or equidistribution.
checks.impact_and_grade: The asserted stronger quantitative estimate for 0<delta<1/2 is not established by the displayed proof. A materially invalid central estimate supports Major without claiming an actual MaaÃŸ-form counterexample or loss of the headline exact-zero result. The report makes these distinctions correctly.

checks.source_claim: The graph definition on pages 17-19, graph transform (6.1) and Lemma 6.1 on pages 28-29, and its use with uniform X_N measure on pages 31-32.
checks.independent_reasoning: Let I be the isolated X vertices. Interchanging finite sums in (6.1) gives total mass sum_(deg x>0)mu(x)=1-mu(I). Because e(x)=empty is a subset of every B, e^-1(Y)=X; Lemma 6.1 would give 1<=1-mu(I). The note that x adjacent to a given y has positive degree does not address absent vertices. For N=21, gamma=[[-6,-5],[17,14]] has determinant 1 and c=17. Left/right integral unipotents give all signed traces 8+17k; the two closest to zero are 8,-9, the next are 25,-26, so no representative has absolute trace in [10.5,21]. This is an actual isolated X_21 vertex under the source definitions. For m>=12, gamma_m=[[m+1,1],[2m+1,2]] has determinant 1 and c=2m+1<=N_m=floor(5(2m+1)/4). The two central progression values m+3 and 2-m have absolute values below N_m/2; the next values 3m+4 and 1-3m exceed N_m in absolute value. Thus isolation also occurs for arbitrarily large N.
checks.counterevidence_and_impact: These finite examples prove failure of the probability normalization and the lower-preimage assertion in the actual construction. They do not determine zeta_N=mu_N(I_N), and therefore do not alone refute the asymptotic Gaussian theorem. The abstract lemma can require zero isolated mass. Conditioning on nonisolated vertices changes interval masses by O(zeta_N) when zeta_N is small, but the application still needs zeta_N=o(1) and an effective rate where claimed, or a revised graph construction. The unweighted edge argument counts isolated vertices with degree zero and is unaffected. Major is appropriately confined to the missing condition in a main weighted-transfer proof route.

checks.source_claim: Lemma 6.2 and its proof, physical PDF 29-30. The actual page-29 image was newly inspected to resolve extraction ambiguity and confirms absolute values around the uniform interval errors.
checks.independent_reasoning: For w_j=2^-j/j, the triangles j(1-|x-3j|/w_j)_+ are disjoint and locally finite, continuous, with total masses j w_j=2^-j summing to 1. Thus F is a fixed continuous probability density with unbounded heights. At each n choose M_n midpoint quantiles with M_n large enough for uniform interval discrepancy <=w_n^2; possible since the CDF is continuous, with endpoint discrepancy bounded by a constant/M_n. A matching between two copies has every degree 1 and normalized transformed mass. Set g_n=f_n+w_n, so the required edge error is exactly E(n)=w_n. On [0,3n], the deficit is integral_(3n-w_n)^(3n)F+O(w_n^2)=n w_n/2+O(w_n^2). Dividing its absolute size by h(n)+E(n), with h(n)<=w_n^2, diverges. This satisfies the general graph lemma's assumptions independently of the isolation problem.
checks.counterevidence_and_impact: For bounded F, the endpoint mass is bounded by ||F||_infinity times the interval length, giving the required O(E) estimate. For general integrable F only its concentration modulus is justified; absolute continuity of the integral makes that modulus tend to zero but not necessarily linearly. The Gaussian application has bounded density, so this is a Minor general-lemma defect. Its correction does not supply missing graph normalization.

checks.source_claim: Theorem 3.5 on page 17 compared with Theorem 1.6 on page 4 and the scales on pages 26-27.
checks.independent_reasoning: The acquired source visibly uses sqrt(log N) in the cited vertical-period CLT and an additional (log log N)^(3/2) in the later Eisenstein argument, corresponding to the stated length scale. The report does not silently pick a correct normalization or count this as a proved theorem failure. The external CLT remains uninspected here, so retaining NeedsEvidence and excluding the Eisenstein deduction from positive certification is honest.
